title: Thymic stromal defects and immune dysregulation in hypomorphic recombinase activating gene (RAG) deficiency: Implications for hematopoietic cell transplantation
abstract: BACKGROUND: Thymic epithelial cells (TECs) are essential for positive and negative selection during T-cell development. Hypomorphic recombinase activating gene (RAG) deficiency is characterized by T-cell lymphopenia and an increased risk of infections and autoimmunity. However, whether abnormalities of TEC composition and function also contribute to these clinical features is unknown. OBJECTIVE: ) mouse model, we examined composition and function of the TEC compartment, both before and after hematopoietic stem cell transplantation. METHODS: Flow cytometry, immunofluorescent imaging, and single-cell RNA sequencing were used to characterize the TECs and thymocytes. Bone marrow transplantation studies were performed to define level of donor chimerism required to fully correct thymic abnormalities. RESULTS: mice fully corrected thymocyte development and normalized the TEC phenotype. However, in competitive settings, lower levels of wild-type hematopoietic stem cell engraftment were associated with persistence of mutant-derived double-negative thymocytes and of a low number of Itgβ4-positive, medullary TEC-low cells, incomplete restoration of the TEC compartment, and autoantibody production. CONCLUSION: mice leads to abnormal TEC composition and immune dysregulation, whose correction requires robust levels of donor chimerism after hematopoietic stem cell transplantation.

title: Systemic Allergic Reactions to mRNA COVID-19 Vaccines: A Randomized Placebo-controlled Trial
abstract: Background COVID-19 mRNA vaccines were associated in early reports with more allergic reactions than most vaccines, especially in people with allergic histories. Objective To estimate the proportions of systemic allergic reactions to mRNA COVID-19 vaccines in people reporting prior severe allergic reactions to various allergens, and/or mast cell disorders (PSAR/MCD Group) and determine if proportions are higher than in non-PSAR/non-MCD (Comparison Group). Methods We conducted a multi-center, randomized, double-blinded (for the initial injection), placebo-controlled trial in PSAR/MCD vs Comparison adults and adolescents. Participants received a double-blinded injection with Pfizer-BioNTech or Moderna COVID-19 vaccine or placebo, followed by unblinded vaccine injections. The primary outcome was the incidence of clinically-determined systemic allergic reactions within 90 minutes after injection. Results The trial enrolled 723 participants of a planned 3400, with 664 (56% PSAR/MCD) receiving at least one injection. Within 90 minutes of injection, systemic allergic reactions occurred in 5/180 (3%) PSAR/MCD participants given Pfizer-BioNTech (vs 0/133 [0%] Comparison Group; p=0.063) and 2/173 (1%) PSAR/MCD participants given Moderna (vs 0/144 [0%] Comparison Group; p=0.27). Reactions were also reported >90 minutes and ≤48 hours only in PSAR/MCD. Among PSAR/MCD participants, reaction rates to vaccine within 90-minutes and 48-hours were similar to placebo. Extensive laboratory studies did not identify plausible reaction mechanisms. Conclusions Systemic allergic reactions based solely on clinical determination within 90-minutes or 48-hours of vaccination were only observed in PSAR/MCD but failure to achieve planned enrollment limited statistical precision. Reactions to placebo and failure to identify underlying immunologic mechanisms suggest non-allergic or non-immunologic causes.

title: Type I autoimmunity in chronic spontaneous urticaria: Evidence, limits, and endotype overlap
abstract: Chronic spontaneous urticaria (CSU) is a mast cell-driven disorder with basophil involvement and several possible upstream mechanisms. Type IIb autoimmune CSU, mediated by functional IgG autoantibodies against FcεRIα or IgE, is the best-validated endotype. Evidence for type I autoimmune (autoallergic) CSU is less complete, but findings involving IgE autoantibodies to thyroid peroxidase (TPO), IL-24, and other self-antigens suggest that IgE-dependent autoreactivity may be relevant in some patients. However, total IgE level, atopy, allergic disease, and timing of the response to omalizumab are not diagnostic of this mechanism. Rather than viewing type I and type IIb CSU as competing categories, we hypothesize 2 potentially overlapping immunologic axes: an IgE-autoantibody axis and an IgG/complement axis. Patients may lie closer to one axis, show markers of both, or remain provisionally idiopathic because current biomarkers cannot classify them with confidence. Progress will require harmonized functional assays; skin, mast cell, and basophil readouts, as well as longitudinal treatment studies. The central question is when an IgE autoantibody is only a passenger, when it is a partner, and when it is the driver of the wheal.

title: Comparative efficacy and safety of antihistamines, increased antihistamine dosing, and antihistamine adjuncts for chronic urticaria: a systematic review, dose-response, and network meta-analysis of randomized trials
abstract: BACKGROUND: Chronic urticaria is a common immune-mediated condition characterized by wheals (itch and hives), angioedema, or both, lasting for greater than six weeks. It is managed with H1 antihistamines as the first-line therapy. Fundamental unresolved questions remain regarding the comparative benefits and harms of antihistamines and their adjuncts, and of H1 antihistamine dose-escalation. OBJECTIVE: To analyze the comparative benefits and harms of antihistamines and their adjuncts (H2 blockers or montelukast), and of H1 antihistamine dose-escalation. METHODS: As part of updating the American Academy of Allergy, Asthma & Immunology and American College of Allergy, Asthma and Immunology Joint Task Force on Practice Parameters Chronic Urticaria guidelines, we searched MEDLINE, EMBASE, CENTRAL, and regulatory databases from inception to March 17, 2025, for randomized trials addressing antihistamines or their adjuncts for chronic urticaria. Paired reviewers independently screened records, extracted data, and assessed risk of bias. Random effects network and dose-response meta-analyses addressed urticaria activity (composed of itch and wheal scores), angioedema activity, urticaria-related quality of life, and harms including sedation. The GRADE approach informed certainty of evidence ratings. PROSPERO: CRD42022367280. RESULTS: 211 trials (22,187 participants) evaluated 55 unique treatments. Bilastine, desloratadine, fexofenadine, and levocetirizine are among the most effective in improving overall urticaria activity, urticaria-related quality of life, and sleep disturbance. Cetirizine and loratadine are among the most effective in reducing overall urticaria activity and its subcomponents, with cetirizine also among the most effective in improving urticaria-related quality of life. Escalating from a single to quadruple daily dose may yield diminishing additional benefit. Second-generation agents as a class may be more effective than first-generation agents in improving urticaria activity and sleep disturbance. Sedation risk likely increases with higher doses, with first-generation agents (e.g., diphenhydramine, hydroxyzine) and doxepin among the most sedating; cetirizine, ketotifen, levocetirizine, and rupatadine among the intermediate sedating; and bepotastine, bilastine, desloratadine, ebastine, fexofenadine, and loratadine among the least sedating. Adding montelukast (moderate certainty) or an H2 blocker (very low certainty) to a second-generation agent may further reduce urticaria activity. CONCLUSIONS: For chronic urticaria, second-generation agents differ in their efficacy and safety. First-generation agents are less beneficial and more harmful. Escalating to higher daily doses may provide additional benefits but likely increases sedation.

title: Lower Nasal Sphingolipids in Pediatric Asthma and Cell-Type-Specific Effects of 17q21 Variants
abstract: Background: Genetic variations at the 17q21 asthma-risk locus regulate GSDMB and ORMDL3, influencing inflammatory pathways and sphingolipid metabolism.Although 17q21 variants such as rs7216389 and rs12936231 are associated with ORMDL3 expression in immune and airway smooth muscle cells, their effects on airway epithelial sphingolipids remain unclear.Objectives: To determine whether asthma or 17q21 asthma genotypes alter sphingolipid composition in the upper respiratory tract in children, and to define contributions of epithelial versus immune cells.Methods: Sphingolipids were quantified by mass spectrometry in nasal fluid and plasma from children with and without asthma.Nasal epithelial cells and PBMCs from healthy adults homozygous for rs7216389 C/C or T/T (risk) were analyzed for sphingolipid levels and ORMDL3/GSDMB associated gene expression.Results: Children with atopic asthma had significantly lower nasal dihydroceramides, ceramides, and sphingosine independent of inhaled corticosteroids and allergic rhinitis.Asthma was associated with increased plasma sphingolipids but decreased sphingolipids in blood cells, mirroring nasal findings.In PBMCs, the rs7216389 T allele was associated with increased ORMDL3 expression and suppressed de-novo sphingolipid synthesis.In nasal epithelial cells, the T allele predominantly increased GSDMB expression and did not alter sphingolipid metabolism.Conclusions: Nasal mucosal sphingolipids are reduced in children with atopic asthma and sphingolipids generated by de-novo sphingolipid synthesis may serve as a noninvasive biomarker of disease.17q21 risk alleles can exert cell-type-specific effects: ORMDL3-mediated suppression of sphingolipid synthesis occurs in immune cells but not in airway epithelial cells. J o u r n a l P r e -p r o o fSystemic immune or inflammatory cell-driven alterations may contribute to reduced airway sphingolipids in asthma. Key Messages• Sphingolipid dysregulation is increasingly recognized as a contributor to asthma, yet sphingolipid composition within the respiratory tract has remained largely unexplored.• We demonstrate that children with atopic asthma have reduced nasal mucosal sphingolipids, independent of corticosteroid use or allergic rhinitis.Genotype-stratified analyses of epithelial cells and PBMCs identifies a cell-type specific effect of a 17q21 risk haplotype: suppression of sphingolipid synthesis occurs in immune cells but not airway epithelium.• These findings establish nasal sphingolipids as a potential biomarker and provide new mechanistic insight into how genetic risk influences asthma pathobiology Capsule Summary: This study demonstrates that 17q21 variants are associated with sphingolipid metabolism in a cell-type-specific manner, establishing a novel link between immune cell sphingolipid metabolism and airway inflammation in childhood asthma.

title: Accounting for seasonal variation of nasal gene expression improves transcriptome analysis of asthma
abstract: INTRODUCTION: Environmental seasonal changes, including allergen exposure, pollutants, and viral prevalence, impact gene expression across human tissues. Therefore, season of sample collection is critical to consider when analyzing disease-associated transcriptional programs. In this study we aimed to investigate the effect of season on identification of asthma-associated genes. METHODS: We analyzed RNA-seq data from nasal brushes of asthma patients (n=361) and healthy controls (n=57) included in the ATLANTIS study. Samples were compared across two time periods defined by a data-driven approach: winter-spring (Nov 15 -May 14) and summer-autumn (May 15 - Nov 14), correcting for age, sex, smoking, and asthma status. Gene Set Variation Analysis (GSVA) scores of the obtained seasonal gene signatures were compared using Mann-Whitney U test in the independent PIAMA cohort (n=325) for replication. RESULTS: We identified 1,731 genes differentially expressed between the two time periods (813 higher and 918 lower in winter-spring compared with summer-autumn; FDR < 0.05). This signature was replicated in the PIAMA cohort nasal gene expression data and was independent of asthma or allergy status. Samples collected in winter-spring showed a significantly lower predicted proportion of ciliated cells (p = 0.005) and a higher proportion of basal cells (p = 0.04) compared to those from summer-autumn. Crucially, including season as a covariate in models for asthma-associated gene expression nearly doubled the number of differentially expressed genes, from 126 to 271 (FDR < 0.05). We conclude that season of sampling strongly affects the nasal transcriptome, and we demonstrate that season-adjusted analyses significantly enhance sensitivity for detecting disease-associated changes.

title: Site-Specific Cutaneous Inflammation: Mechanisms and Therapeutic Implications
abstract: Inflammatory skin diseases exhibit prominent anatomical distribution patterns that have long guided clinical diagnosis, yet the biological mechanisms underlying site specificity remain incompletely defined. These regional predilections arise from structural, immunological, and microbial heterogeneity across human skin. Epidermal barrier architecture, which varies substantially between body sites, including 10- to 100-fold differences in stratum corneum thickness, and prevalence and types of hair follicles and glands, creates distinct microenvironments that shape resident immune populations, microbial communities and host antimicrobial defenses. The skin harbors an estimated 20 billion tissue-resident memory T cells that persist within anatomically restricted niches, providing a mechanistic basis for disease recurrence at the same sites. In parallel, the skin microbiome contributes to regional specialization by forming distinct communities in oily, moist, and dry regions, which are disrupted in disease-specific ways, while environmental exposures such as ultraviolet radiation, mechanical stress, and humidity further reinforce regional variation. Recent advances in single-cell and spatial transcriptomic technologies have enabled inflammatory responses to be mapped with high precision, allowing detailed interrogation of site-specific cellular interactions and signaling pathways across the skin. Collectively, these findings support a unifying model in which regional tissue properties and local immune ecosystems shape disease-specific inflammatory circuits, accounting for the anatomical predilection of inflammatory diseases and underscoring the importance of tissue context for precision therapeutics.

title: IFN-γ-NOD2/IL-5-FCGR axis enhances eosinophil extracellular trap formation in allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis/mycosis
abstract: BACKGROUND: Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis/mycosis (ABPA/M) is characterized by systemic eosinophilia and eosinophil-rich mucus plugs, but mechanisms programming eosinophil pathogenicity remain unclear. OBJECTIVE: We aim to define eosinophil activation programs and upstream signals that promote extracellular trap formation in ABPA/M. METHODS: We performed multi-omics analyses (RNA sequencing and proteomics) of blood eosinophils from healthy participants, patients with eosinophilic asthma, and patients with ABPA/M. Surface-marker profiles were compared between blood and airway eosinophils from patients with ABPA/M. In vitro stimulation assays using IFN-γ, IL-5, and a nucleotide-binding oligomerization domain-containing 2 (NOD2) ligand were combined with multi-omics readouts and functional evaluation of IgG cross-linking-induced eosinophil extracellular trap formation. RESULTS: Multi-omics profiling identified activation patterns consistent with IFN-γ and IL-5 signaling in ABPA/M blood eosinophils. ICAM-1 was upregulated on both blood and airway eosinophils, whereas PD-L1 upregulation was specific to airway eosinophils. PD-L1 induction required combined stimulation with IFN-γ and a NOD2 ligand, but not IL-5. Under IFN-γ plus NOD2 ligand stimulation, eosinophils exhibited inflammatory remodeling, including increased Fc gamma receptor expression. Functionally, pretreatment with IFN-γ and a NOD2 ligand enhanced IgG cross-linking-induced extracellular trap formation in an NADPH oxidase-dependent manner and required lymphocyte function-associated antigen 1 interactions with ICAM-1. Combined stimulation with IFN-γ and IL-5 similarly augmented extracellular trap formation. CONCLUSION: ABPA/M eosinophils are shaped by mixed inflammatory cues, in which IFN-γ cooperates with fungal-sensing signals or IL-5 to enhance Fc gamma receptor-linked, IgG-triggered extracellular trap formation, potentially contributing to mucus plugging.

title: Comparative efficacy and safety of treatments for eosinophilic esophagitis: Systematic review and network meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
abstract: BACKGROUND: Eosinophilic esophagitis (EoE) is a chronic immune-mediated disease characterized by esophageal dysfunction and eosinophilic inflammation. Comparative efficacy and safety of therapies remain uncertain. OBJECTIVE: To compare efficacy and safety of treatments for EoE in children and adults. METHODS: We conducted a systematic review and network meta-analysis (NMA) of randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing pharmacologic, dietary, and mechanical interventions. We searched MEDLINE, EMBASE, and CENTRAL to March 17, 2026. Reviewers screened studies, extracted data, and assessed risk of bias. We conducted random-effects NMA; assessed certainty using GRADE. RESULTS: We included 48 RCTs (3,963 participants). High-frequency dupilumab [mean difference (MD) -11.08, 95% confidence interval (CI) -15.14 to -7.03; high certainty] and swallowed topical corticosteroids (STCs) (MD -6.86, 95%CI -9.17 to -4.56; moderate certainty) are likely among the most effective for symptoms. Similarly, high-frequency dupilumab (MD 6.57, 95%CI 3.42 to 9.71; moderate certainty) and STCs (MD 7.20, 95%CI 1.01 to 13.39; moderate certainty) are among the most effective for quality-of-life. Certain biologics and epicutaneous immunotherapy are likely not different from placebo for symptoms (moderate certainty). Multiple interventions reduce peak eosinophil counts (high certainty) and likely do not increase harms versus placebo (moderate or high certainty). Four- and six-food elimination diets (FEDs) may be better than 1FED for symptoms (low certainty), but not other outcomes, with greater burden. CONCLUSIONS: High-frequency dupilumab and STCs are among the most effective therapies across patient-important and inflammatory outcomes. Histologic improvements do not guarantee patient-important outcome improvement. FED benefits are modest and low certainty, and traded off by burdens.

title: Refining atopic dermatitis pathogenesis: Early-life trajectories, noncanonical cytokines, and JAK–STAT signaling
abstract: Atopic dermatitis (AD) is increasingly understood as a biologically heterogeneous disease in which barrier dysfunction, type 2 inflammation, neuroimmune dysregulation, and intracellular signaling abnormalities interact in dynamic and context-dependent ways. This review highlights three concepts that have advanced the field in recent years. First, studies in early life suggest that AD harbors measurable preclinical abnormalities, developmental trajectories, and potential opportunities for targeted intervention. Second, recent work has refined the cytokine architecture of AD beyond interleukin (IL)-4 and IL-13 by identifying noncanonical cytokine circuits that shape distinct aspects of the disease phenotype, including upstream pathogenic T helper type 2 (TH2) cell activation, epidermal dysfunction, and itch. Third, rare gain-of-function (GOF) disorders involving signal transducer and activator of transcription 6 (STAT6) and Janus kinase 1 (JAK1) have consolidated the relevance of the IL-4/IL-13-JAK-STAT signaling axis in AD, providing insight into how specific alterations within this axis can drive severe allergic skin disease and associated systemic phenotypes. Considered together, these developments support a more differentiated view of AD pathophysiology, in which disease onset, tissue inflammation, barrier impairment, pruritus, and therapeutic response are governed by partially overlapping but nonidentical pathways.

title: Precision Diagnosis and Differentiation of Eosinophilic Colitis and Inflammatory Bowel Disease Using a Tissue-Based Molecular Gene Expression Panel
abstract: BACKGROUND: Eosinophilic colitis (EoC) and eosinophil-predominant inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) can show overlapping clinical and histologic features, creating diagnostic uncertainty. Whether tissue gene expression can objectively distinguish these conditions in the setting of colonic eosinophilia remains unclear. OBJECTIVE: We sought to develop and validate a tissue-based molecular diagnostic panel to quantify eosinophilic inflammation and differentiate EoC from IBD-associated colonic eosinophilia. METHODS: This multi-center study analyzed 88 colonic biopsies from a cohort enriched for children and young adults, including 74 patients with EoC or IBD and non-disease controls. We developed a 96-gene qPCR-based platform, the Colonic Eosinophilia Diagnostic Panel (CEDP), and generated molecular EoC and IBD scores. Diagnostic accuracy was determined by area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC). RESULTS: An EoC score developed from 59 genes (e.g., eosinophil-associated gene CLC) distinguished active EoC from non-disease controls (AUC 0.92, 95% CI 0.78-1.0) and quantified the active molecular eosinophilic inflammatory program, correlating with peak eosinophil counts. However, this score did not differentiate EoC from IBD. An IBD score from 18 genes (e.g., DUOXA2) reflecting inflammatory pathways provided complementary discriminatory information and resolved this overlap. This approach distinguished active IBD from all other groups (AUC 0.98, 95% CI 0.76-1.0) and specifically active EoC (AUC 0.99, 95% CI 0.95-1.0), correlated with endoscopic activity, and differentiated IBD with high colonic eosinophil counts. CONCLUSIONS: We developed the CEDP with a tissue-based, two-component molecular framework for evaluating colonic eosinophilia. By measuring eosinophilic inflammatory activity and identifying an IBD-associated molecular signature, this platform can distinguish EoC from IBD beyond conventional histopathology alone.

title: Downregulation of SIRT3 Activates Macrophage Proinflammatory Function and Exacerbates Olfactory Loss in a Mouse Model of Chronic Rhinosinusitis
abstract: Background Inflammation of the olfactory mucosa, rather than airflow obstruction, is a major barrier to olfactory recovery in chronic rhinosinusitis with olfactory dysfunction (CRSwOD). Macrophages, a predominant immune cell population in the olfactory mucosa, play a key role in regulating local inflammation and olfactory neuroregeneration. Objective This study aimed to investigate the role of Sirtuin 3 (SIRT3) in modulating macrophage function and its impact on olfactory recovery in CRSwOD. Methods Single-cell RNA sequencing, bulk RNA sequencing, and untargeted metabolomics data were analyzed to characterize immune and neuronal alterations in CRSwOD, with a focus on macrophage activation states. In vivo experiments using SIRT3-deficient mice were performed to evaluate olfactory sensory neuron (OSN) integrity, while in vitro assays examined the metabolic and inflammatory profiles of SIRT3-deficient macrophages under inflammatory conditions. Results Transcriptomic analysis revealed that olfactory dysfunction was closely associated with the altered functional status of mucosal macrophages. During the progression of chronic rhinosinusitis in mice, loss of SIRT3 exacerbated OSN loss and impaired the protective role of macrophages in maintaining neuronal homeostasis. Mechanistically, SIRT3 deficiency enhanced macrophage proinflammatory activity, increased hypoxia-inducible factor 1α (HIF-1α) expression, promoted glycolysis, and reduced mitochondrial membrane potential. Conclusion In a mouse model of chronic rhinosinusitis, SIRT3 modulates macrophage-mediated inflammatory metabolism within the olfactory mucosa, thereby protecting against inflammation-induced olfactory damage. These findings provide mechanistic insight into inflammation-driven olfactory dysfunction and identify SIRT3 as a potential therapeutic target for CRSwOD.

title: Do School Food Allergy Policies Harm or Help? Quality of Life, Anxiety, and Bullying in Children with Peanut and Tree Nut Allergy
abstract: Background Food allergy (FA) restrictive policies (RPs) are widely used in daycares/schools, but clinicians and families worry policies may increase stigma, bullying, or anxiety; these psychosocial effects have not been characterized. Objective We sought to examine how FA RPs in daycares/schools impact the psychosocial wellbeing of children with IgE-mediated FA and their parents. Methods We conducted a survey of child-parent pairs recruited from Boston Children's Hospital and through social media. Participants completed self-administered electronic surveys on daycare/school FA policies and validated instruments assessing FA-related psychosocial wellbeing. Inclusion criteria were children aged Results The cohort included 652 child-parent dyads. Parents were primarily mothers (96.7%). Median child age was 6.0 years. Across all grades, there was no association between presence of RPs and parental FA-related QOL, parent or child FA-related anxiety, or FA-related bullying. In young children, presence of RPs was associated with higher FA-related quality of life (QOL) (daycare/preschool/pre-K p=0.007, elementary p=0.048); no association was found in older children. Presence of any RP was associated with greater parental comfort with FA policies across all grades (p Conclusion We found no evidence that FA RPs impact bullying, FA-related anxiety, or general anxiety among children or their parents. However, FA RPs improved FA-related QOL in younger children. These findings provide novel evidence-based data to inform school FA policy design.

title: Self-reported health history from 70,724 individuals reveals novel HLA associations with allergy and other frequently underreported conditions
abstract: Background Variation in the HLA loci, located on human chromosome 6p, has been associated with hundreds of diseases and conditions. However, high levels of polymorphism that characterize the HLA system, coupled with generally modest effect sizes for most phenotypes, necessitate relatively large sample sizes to power association studies; meanwhile, high resolution HLA genotyping remains relatively resource intensive. These constraints limit identification of novel associations. While phenome-wide association studies (PheWAS) in the context of large registries with available electronic health records (EHR) have revealed new insights into the role of HLA in disease, many common health conditions are poorly represented in EHR due to the temporal nature of their occurrence or general underreporting. Further, these studies have generally been conducted with HLA genotyping data imputed from microarrays, rather than direct measurement of high-resolution genotypes. Objective To overcome these limitations and reveal novel HLA associations we undertook a PheWAS in many previously understudied health conditions. Methods We queried over 290 conditions, diseases and traits from 70,724 subjects registered with NMDP (formerly known as the National Marrow Donor Program) with available high-resolution HLA genotyping (HLA-A, HLA-B, HLA-C, HLA-DRB1, and HLA-DQB1). After stratifying according to self-reported geographic ancestry, we performed a logistic regression analysis adjusting for sex and age for HLA-phenotype association. Results We identified 48 significant HLA associations across self-reported geographic ancestry groups, confirming several known associations and uncovered fourteen novel associations. Most novel associations pertained to common infectious or allergic phenotypes that often go under-reported in the EHR. We identified a previously underappreciated yet very strong association between HLA-DRB1*04:01 and self-reported cefaclor adverse-reaction label of unverified mechanism (OR = 3.74, p-value 5.10E-28), which remained highly significant after excluding individuals reporting multiple drug hypersensitivities (OR = 3.13, p-value = 5.60E-15). Exploratory computational co-folding structure-and-affinity prediction identified a potential interaction between cefaclor and the P4 pocket of HLA-DRB1*04:01, providing a hypothesis-generating structural rationale that requires functional validation. If validated in independent cohorts with clinically characterized phenotypes and functional studies, this association may inform pharmacogenomic risk stratification and targeted prevention of adverse drug reactions. Other novel associations found, such as susceptibility to genital warts (HPV) and allergic rhinitis, reveal new insights into the role of specific HLA alleles in immune-mediated disease. Many of these novel associations were replicated in the independent All of Us cohort (AoU), while others showed the same trend for association, confirming the validity of this approach. Conclusion Collectively, our findings demonstrate the value of integrating population-scale, high-resolution HLA genotypes with phenotyping beyond the EHR to reveal immunogenetic influences on common health outcomes. These findings motivate future functional studies and validation in clinically characterized cohorts to refine mechanistic understanding and determine potential clinical utility.

title: Persistent indirect airway hyperresponsiveness after six weeks of high-dose inhaled corticosteroids identifies a subgroup with higher T2 inflammation and mast cell burden
abstract: BACKGROUND: Indirect airway hyperresponsiveness (AHR) to osmotic stimuli such as mannitol is a hallmark of asthma and typically improves with inhaled corticosteroids (ICS), in contrast to direct AHR stimuli (e.g. methacholine), which often persists despite treatment. Persistent indirect AHR (PIAHR) after high-dose ICS may reflect incomplete suppression of airway inflammation. OBJECTIVE: We aimed to characterise clinical, inflammatory, and tissue features associated with persistent indirect AHR in patients with asthma before and after high-dose ICS treatment. METHODS: <635 mg). RESULTS: After six weeks of ICS, 11/46 patients (24%) had PIAHR. At baseline, incomplete responders had more severe AHR and higher type 2 (T2) biomarker levels including FeNO, blood- and sputum eosinophils as well as a higher density of airway chymase-positive mast cells. Despite reductions in T2 markers in both groups, incomplete responders exhibited higher blood- and sputum eosinophils after six weeks treatment. Airway mast cell and eosinophil densities decreased similarly, but reductions in blood eosinophils were smaller in incomplete responders. CONCLUSION: PIAHR after six weeks of high-dose ICS is associated with incomplete suppression of T2 inflammation and mast cell-associated features. This pattern may help identify patients in whom airway inflammation is incompletely controlled by ICS alone and who may benefit from closer follow-up or further targeted treatment.

title: The metabolic reprogramming of T cells controls airway remodeling in severe asthma
abstract: Abstract Mixed granulocytic asthma (MGA) is a severe Th2-low endotype, characterized by high Th17/neutrophilic burden and exacerbated airway remodeling. Both features confer resistance to inhaled corticosteroids, and typical asthma treatments. Thus, MGA is an enormous public health burden. Gaps in knowledge include how Th17 cells induce pathological tissue remodeling, and how Th17 differentiation occurs in response to allergens. We generated a Th2-low murine model of asthma that recapitulates major features of human MGA namely, heightened airway reactivity to methacholine, Th17/neutrophilic inflammation, airway remodeling, and resistance to corticosteroid treatment. Two specific biomarkers enriched in human MGA, the TNF superfamily member 14 (aka LIGHT), and the mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) pathway, are upregulated in this model. We show OXPHOS promotes the metabolic reprograming of Th17 cells, to produce LIGHT that controls airway remodeling. Mechanistically, OXPHOS regulates RORγt expression and the subsequent transcriptional network to program survival and differentiation of Th17 cells, whereas LIGHT drives airway remodeling by activating the MMP9-dependent TGFβ pathway. Additionally, OXPHOS + Th17 cells promote the expression of osteopontin necessary for fibroblast activation. LIGHT antagonistic blockade reduces airway remodeling, whereas OXPHOS chemical inhibition reduces Th17 cells and neutrophilia. Importantly, the dual blockade of LIGHT and OXPHOS reverses all features of MGA and reciprocally increase the numbers of Treg cells. Thus, the dual blockade of LIGHT and OXPHOS constitutes a promising target for clinical interventions in human MGA, possibly extending to other Th17-driven fibrotic diseases.

title: Persistent Pain in Pediatric Eosinophilic Esophagitis: Evidence for a Distinct Clinical Subtype
abstract: BACKGROUND: Eosinophilic esophagitis (EoE) is a chronic, food antigen-driven inflammatory esophageal disease associated with diverse symptoms, including pain, which has received little attention. METHODS: We performed a retrospective, case-control study of 1,097 patients with EoE treated at Cincinnati Children's Hospital. Patients with documented, persistent EoE-associated pain were identified using a validated natural language processing algorithm. Following systematic review and abstraction of the electronic health record of patients with EoE-associated persistent pain (EoEp+) and no documented EoE-associated pain (EoEp-), a nested subgroup of confirmed subjects (n = 47 per group) was examined for clinical features and esophageal gene expression. RESULTS: Clinically significant EoEp+ represented 4.3% of EoE subjects. Demographics, disease activity including eosinophil levels, and dysphagia were similar between groups; however, patients with EoEp+ were older at initial presentation (13.01 vs. 7.997 years, p < 0.028). Within the EoEp+ phenotype, duration of EoE care is associated with increasing endoscopy burden over time (r = 0.68, p < 0.0001). Subjects with EoEp+ most commonly experienced abdominal pain-38% isolated pain and 62% with additional gastrointestinal symptoms-and experienced more polytherapy (p = 0.0020), treatment alteration (p = 0.027), and comorbid conditions than subjects with EoEp-. Gene expression analyses revealed decreased ALOX15 levels in EoEp+ esophageal biopsies, particularly in remission cases (p = 0.0062). CONCLUSIONS: Persistent pain in pediatric EoE is associated with a distinct clinical profile, characterized by greater treatment complexity, increased comorbid conditions, and dysregulated ALOX15 expression. These findings suggest that persistent pain in EoE identifies a clinically meaningful candidate endotype and highlights the need for targeted management strategies.
